blocks.text: K. wondered whether he ought not to slip away now in all haste; if he did not do so now, there was no prospect that he could do so during the sermon, he would then have to stay as long as it lasted, he was losing so much time at the office, he had long ceased to be under any obligation to wait for the Italian, he looked at his watch, it was eleven. But could a sermon really be delivered? Could K. alone represent the congregation? What if he had been a stranger who merely wanted to view the church? At bottom he was nothing else. It was absurd to think that a sermon was to be preached, now at eleven o’clock, on a weekday in the most abominable weather. The priest—a priest he undoubtedly was, a young man with a smooth, dark face—was obviously only going up in order to put out the lamp, which had been lit by mistake.

Yet it was not so, on the contrary the priest examined the light and turned it up a little higher still, then he turned slowly toward the balustrade, which he gripped in front by its angular rim with both hands. So he stood for a while and looked about him without moving his head. K. had retreated a great distance and was leaning with his elbows on the foremost pew. With uncertain eyes he saw somewhere, without determining the spot precisely, the verger with bent back crouching down peacefully as if after a completed task. What a stillness now reigned in the cathedral! Yet K. was obliged to disturb it, he had no intention of staying here; if it was the priest’s duty to preach at a fixed hour without regard to the circumstances, let him do so, it would succeed without K.’s assistance too, just as K.’s presence would certainly not heighten the effect. Slowly, therefore, K. set himself in motion, felt his way on tiptoe along the pew, then came out into the broad central aisle and walked along there too quite undisturbed, save that the stone floor rang out beneath the lightest step and the vaults echoed from it faintly, yet continuously, in manifold, regular progression. K. felt a little forsaken as he walked along there alone between the empty pews, observed perhaps by the priest, and the size of the cathedral too seemed to him to lie right on the border of what was still endurable for human beings. When he came to his former place, without pausing further he fairly snatched at the album he had left lying there and took it with him. He had almost left the region of the pews and was approaching the open space that lay between them and the exit when for the first time he heard the priest’s voice. A powerful, practised voice. How it penetrated the cathedral waiting in readiness to receive it! Yet it was not the congregation that the priest called upon, it was quite unmistakable and there were no evasions, he called out: “Josef K.!”

K. halted and looked down at the floor before him. For the time being he was still free, he could still walk on and make his escape through one of the three small dark wooden doors that were not far in front of him. It would simply mean that he had not understood, or that he had indeed understood, yet did not wish to pay any heed to it. Should he turn round, however, he was caught, for then he would have made the confession that he had understood well enough, that he was really the person called upon, and that he also meant to obey. Had the priest called out once more, K. would certainly have gone away, but since all remained silent, however long K. waited, he did turn his head a little after all, for he wanted to see what the priest was doing now. He was standing quietly in the pulpit as before, yet it was plain to see that he had noticed the turn of K.’s head. It would have been a childish game of hide-and-seek if K. had not now turned round completely. He did so and was beckoned nearer by the priest with a motion of his finger. Since everything could now be done openly, he ran—he did so out of curiosity as well and in order to cut the matter short—with long flying strides toward the pulpit. At the first pews he came to a halt, but to the priest the distance still seemed too great, he stretched out his hand and pointed with his sharply lowered forefinger to a spot close in front of the pulpit. K. obeyed in this too; standing in this place he already had to bend his head far back in order still to see the priest. “You are Josef K.,” said the priest, raising one hand on the balustrade in an indeterminate gesture. “Yes,” said K.; he thought of how frankly he had always given his name in the past, for some time now it had been a burden to him, and now people with whom he came together for the first time knew his name as well; how pleasant it had been to introduce oneself first and only then to be known. “You are an accused man,” said the priest particularly softly. “Yes,” said K., “I have been informed of that.” “Then you are the man I am looking for,” said the priest. “I am the prison chaplain.” “Ah, I see,” said K. “I had you summoned here,” said the priest, “in order to speak with you.” “I did not know that,” said K. “I came here in order to show the cathedral to an Italian.” “Leave essentials aside,” said the priest. “What are you holding in your hand? Is it a prayer-book?” “No,” answered K., “it is an album of the sights of the town.” “Lay it out of your hand,” said the priest. K. threw it away so violently that it flew open and trailed a little way across the floor with crumpled leaves. “Do you know that your case stands badly?” asked the priest. “It seems so to me too,” said K. “I have taken every possible trouble, but hitherto without success. To be sure, I have not finished my petition yet.” “How do you picture the end?” asked the priest. “At first I thought it must end well,” said K., “now I sometimes doubt it myself. I do not know how it will end. Do you know?” “No,” said the priest, “but I fear it will end badly. You are considered guilty. Your case will perhaps not even get beyond a lower court. Look you, for the time being at least, your guilt is considered proven.” “Yet I am not guilty,” said K. “It is a mistake. How can a human being ever be guilty at all? We are all human beings here, after all, one like another.” “That is right,” said the priest, “but that is how the guilty are wont to talk.” “Are you prejudiced against me too?” asked K. “I have no prejudice against you,” said the priest. “I thank you,” said K. “Yet all the others who are involved in the proceedings have a prejudice against me. They instill it into the uninvolved as well. My position grows more and more difficult.” “You misunderstand the facts,” said the priest. “The verdict does not come all at once, the proceedings gradually merge into the verdict.” “So that is how it is,” said K., lowering his head. “What do you mean to do next in your affair?” asked the priest. “I mean to seek further help,” said K., raising his head to see how the priest judged this. “There are still certain possibilities of which I have not availed myself.” “You seek too much outside help,” said the priest disapprovingly, “and especially from women. Do you not notice that it is not the true help?” “Sometimes and even often I could agree with you,” said K., “but not always. Women have great power. If I could prevail upon a few women whom I know to work for me in common, I could not fail to win through. Especially before this court, which consists almost entirely of woman-chasers. Show the examining magistrate a woman in the distance and he will bowl over the court table and the accused simply in order to get there in time.” The priest bent his head toward the balustrade; only now did the canopy of the pulpit seem to press him down. What sort of tempest could there be outside? It was no longer a dull day, it was already deep night. No stained glass in the great windows was able to break the dark wall with even a single glimmer. And at this very moment the verger began to put out the candles on the high altar one after another. “Are you angry with me?” K. asked the priest. “Perhaps you do not know what sort of court you serve.” He received no answer. “These are only my own experiences, after all,” said K. Up above all still remained silent. “I did not mean to insult you,” said K. Then the priest cried down to K.: “Can you not see two paces in front of you?” It was cried in wrath, yet at the same time like the cry of one who sees someone fall and, because he is startled himself, cries out rashly, against his own will.
